transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Liam, Sofia (Redwood); Elena, Marcus, Priya (Sentinel)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off the quantization review. I know Elena is especially interested in accuracy regressions when moving to int8 or more aggressive formats. Quick intros?

[00:15] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Hi all, yeah, thanks. We're evaluating options to reduce token cost and increase throughput for our inference tier. Primary concerns: accuracy drift on our NER/classification heads, and latency p95 under 300ms for chat flows.

[00:30] Liam Chen: Cool, I'll lead the deep dive. Quick agenda: cover INT8/FP8 tradeoffs, GPTQ / AWQ algorithms, where regressions tend to come from, how KV cache and batching interact with quantized kernels, and what to expect on VPC/on-prem installs.

[01:00] Priya Nair: Also want to understand operational constraints  do we need specific CUDA/toolkit versions, and how does KMS integrate on-prem.

[02:10] Liam Chen: Right, big picture: FP8 preserves more dynamic range than int8, so in many cases FP8 is safer for accuracy  but FP8 kernels are younger, less optimized on some stacks so throughput might be lower. INT8, especially with GPTQ-style post-training quantization, can give significant throughput and memory wins but you often trade off some accuracy, particularly with outlier rows in attention or LayerNorm.

[03:20] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Can you give examples of where INT8 fails?

[03:45] Liam Chen: Sure  common failure modes: per-channel scales that don't capture heavy-tail weights, quantization noise in Q/K/V projections causing softmax temperature shifts, and biases in output layers. Also generative models can show subtle token-level divergence causing downstream NER F1 drop. We've seen a few models lose ~1-3% F1 after naive int8 without calibration.

[04:40] Marcus Lee: What about GPTQ vs AWQ? We saw a tweet thread but not sure differences in practice.

[05:05] Liam Chen: GPTQ (G P T Q) is a blockwise, second-order method focusing on reconstructing activations; it can preserve quality quite well but it's more compute-heavy to produce the quantized checkpoint. AWQ (A W Q) is a newer approach that often gives similar accuracy with faster runtime conversion and is tuned for int8 kernels; both have tradeoffs. In our internal tests, GPTQ tends to be slightly better on very large decoders for perplexity, while AWQ has better runtime compatibility on some GPU kernels.

[06:30] Sofia Martinez: Add to that  some models benefit from mixed approaches: keep first and last layers in fp16/32 and quantize the middle. That often reduces regressions.

[07:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Do you have numbers? Like latency/throughput with int8/gptq vs fp8 baseline?

[07:25] Liam Chen: We shared a summary in the demo deck  but quick ballpark from our bench: for a 7B decoder model on A100, fp16 baseline gives X tokens/s ~ 1200 t/s and p95 latency for 32-token responses ~ 240ms. INT8 (GPTQ) via optimized kernels can increase t/s to ~2000-2200 and p95 drops to ~160-180ms for same batch, but note that those are for ideal batchable workloads. FP8 (with experimental kernels) landed around 1500 t/s but with higher variance depending on CUDA/cuDNN version. These are illustrative; we'll run your exact prompts.

[08:35] Marcus Lee: When you say "ideal batchable"  our app often tries to keep latency low so batch sizes are 1-4. How does batching affect quantized performance?

[09:00] Liam Chen: At small batch sizes the per-request overhead dominates. INT8 kernels are still faster due to smaller memory footprint and better cache utilization, but the win shrinks. The sweet spot for throughput wins is batching 8-32 tokens across requests. Continuous batching and request coalescing (what our runtime does) helps, but that depends on your tail latency SLOs.

[10:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: How does KV cache interact with quantization? Any gotchas?

[10:20] Liam Chen: KV cache is orthogonal to weight quantization  it's about cached activations. But two interactions: 1) Quantized kernels can change the numerical output slightly so cache hit heuristics and prefix caching need careful validation  you may get divergence faster if cached states were created under different numeric regime. 2) Memory improvements from int8 mean you can keep larger caches on GPU which helps throughput. We recommend validating end-to-end with full convo histories to surface drift.

[11:30] Priya Nair: For on-prem, what kernel dependencies are required?

[11:50] Liam Chen: Depends on format. INT8/GPTQ kernels rely on CUTLASS/accelerated matrix kernels and specific CUDA/CuBLAS and sometimes cuDNN versions. FP8 often needs the latest CUDA + cuDNN and sometimes compiler flags. We'll share an environment matrix but main note: if you're on older drivers you might not get the optimized paths; fallback to slower generic kernels. Also MKL/oneDNN are relevant for CPU-only fallback.

[13:10] Dr. Elena Ruiz: What about deterministic behavior and auditing  do quantized runs affect reproducibility?

[13:30] Liam Chen: Slightly. Reduced precision can increase nondeterminism especially when fused kernels and different math libraries are used. For audit trails we recommend capturing seed/driver/kernel versions and store per-request logits for a sample of traffic. Redwood's rollout tooling can do A/B between fp16 and quantized variants and do automatic quality regression checks on your eval prompts.

[14:40] Sofia Martinez: Also worth mentioning: when doing rolling rollouts we recommend canary with sample weights for critical prompts. If you have a safety or NER-sensitive route, don't swap model format globally without verifying metrics.

[15:10] Marcus Lee: On security: KMS/HSM integration  if we do on-prem with customer-managed keys how does Redwood integrate?

[15:30] Maya Patel: For Private we support KMS integrations and HSM flows; we can point you to our security docs. For on-prem we support customer-managed keys and we log encryption usage  we'll share SOC2 artifacts as part of the packet.

[16:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Great. About accuracy regressions  you mentioned calibration sets earlier, how big should they be?

[16:20] Liam Chen: Usually a 1k-10k sample calibration set representative of your distribution is good. For heavy-tail tokens or sparse classes you may need stratified sampling  e.g., more NER examples. The calibration set is used for per-channel scale selection and can drop a lot of regressions. We'll need a few thousand in your case since you're sensitive on F1.

[17:15] Priya Nair: Any recommended quantization config? Like per-channel vs per-tensor, symmetric vs asymmetric?

[17:35] Liam Chen: Per-channel asymmetric is often best for attention projections; per-tensor might be OK for FFN. Symmetric quant works better for kernels optimized for int8 GEMM. Also keep LayerNorm/softmax in fp16/32. We include config templates in the benchmark repo we'll share.

[18:30] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Can Redwood run the conversions and bench on our behalf? We have limited infra capacity right now.

[18:50] Maya Patel: Yes, we can run an initial pass  Liam will run GPTQ and AWQ conversions on a sample of your prompts and return throughput/accuracy delta. We'll need the calibration set plus instructions on eval metrics.

[19:10] Liam Chen: Practical note: conversion times vary  GPTQ on a 13B can take a few hours on a single A100; AWQ conversions often complete faster. We'll provide time estimates in the spreadsheet.

[20:00] Priya Nair: For on-prem kernel compatibility testing  do you need root access to our clusters?

[20:20] Marcus Lee: We can't give root, but we can spin up a test cluster or provide VM images.

[20:35] Liam Chen: We can work with your SREs to install a test agent in user space; full perf tuning might need drivers upgrades which you control. For privacy we can do the conversion in our environment if you provide a sanitized model or let us run with blinded prompts.

[21:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: What about model licensing  if we use a quantized checkpoint do you need to re-check license?

[21:20] Maya Patel: Good question. That depends on the upstream model license; we can help verify but legal needs to sign off on distribution for us to host derived quantized checkpoints. We'll add that as an item.

[22:10] [short side discussion about scheduling PoC]

[24:00] Liam Chen: Back to perf  KV cache warmup: when you keep long conversations, the cache size grows  int8 reduces mem pressure but watch out for context window extremes. Also batch composition matters: heterogeneous prompt lengths can cause fragmentation; our runtime supports dynamic bucketing to mitigate that.

[26:30] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Any unexpected accuracy regressions you've seen with AWQ?

[26:50] Liam Chen: Less common than naive int8, but AWQ sometimes struggles on models trained with heavy quantization-aware training or with certain activations (GELU approximations). Again, calibration and mixed-precision fixes this in most cases.

[28:00] Priya Nair: Should we consider FP8 given the hardware roadmap? We're evaluating new racks with H100s.

[28:20] Liam Chen: H100 makes FP8 more attractive; if you'll run on H100s FP8 latency/throughput is promising. But if you need broad compatibility across A100/consumer GPUs, int8/GPTQ/AWQ might be safer. FP8 also has less maturity in some operator libraries.

[30:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Great  let's talk about the benchmarking plan and deliverables.

[30:20] Maya Patel: Plan: 1) Sentinel provides 2k calibration samples + 1k eval prompts (NER-focused). 2) Redwood converts and runs three variants: fp16 baseline, GPTQ int8, AWQ int8 (and optional FP8 on H100 if you provide env). 3) Return a spreadsheet with p50/p95 latencies, tokens/s, memory usage, and accuracy deltas (F1/perplexity). 4) Follow-up call to review results and plan next steps.

[32:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: That works for us. Timeline?

[32:10] Maya Patel: We'll aim for initial results within one week of receiving the datasets  Liam will estimate conversion runtime in the sheet.

[33:20] Marcus Lee: One more operational Q: how do you handle fallbacks  if quantized route fails do you have automatic failover to fp16?

[33:40] Liam Chen: Yes, Redwood runtime supports policy-based routing and automatic fallback. You can set thresholds on quality metrics and latency. If a canary flags regression we can route a percentage back to fp16 or to a different model.

[34:10] Priya Nair: Will logs include per-request model variant info for debugging?

[34:30] Maya Patel: Yes, we log model version/format and runtime kernels used. We can increase retention for the pilot.

[35:00] [10 minute technical discussion between Liam and Marcus about driver versions, specific kernel flags and how to capture counters  partially mis-attributed in transcript]

[45:30] Liam Chen: Quick note  sometimes transcripts show as "Speaker 1" but that was me on the deep-dive. Apologies for any mis-labels.

[46:00] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Ok, next steps recap?

[46:10] Maya Patel: Recap: Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet + security doc links; Sentinel to share calibration/eval sets; Redwood SE to run GPTQ/AWQ conversions and report results; schedule PoC planning call week of 2026-03-16.

[46:40] Dr. Elena Ruiz: Thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.

[47:00] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone  we'll follow up in email with links (benchmarks, security packet, and a short runbook).

[47:15] [end call]

Notes: rough transcription; occasional word swaps (e.g., "K V cash" vs "KV cache"), some speaker labels generic. Shared artifacts: link to benchmark spreadsheet (private), link to security packet (SOC2/ISO) and conversion scripts repo (internal).
